sections.text: A kidney-friendly diet is not one fixed menu. It is an eating pattern adjusted to your kidney function, blood test results and medicines, and the main nutrients that may need attention in chronic kidney disease (CKD) are sodium, potassium, phosphorus and protein. The NIDDK and the National Kidney Foundation (NKF) both say the right amounts depend on the person and recommend working with a registered dietitian, ideally one who specialises in kidney disease. This page summarises what those sources say. It does not give you a personal prescription.

Do not start restricting or adding any nutrient, supplement or fluid amount on the strength of a web page. Needs differ widely by CKD stage, urine protein, blood potassium and phosphorus levels, medicines and whether you are on dialysis. Ask your nephrologist or renal dietitian for your own targets.
Why diet matters when kidney function drops

Healthy kidneys remove waste and balance minerals. When filtration is reduced, some of those substances can build up. The NIDDK says choosing healthy foods and avoiding too much sodium, potassium and phosphorus may prevent or delay some CKD problems. You can see where you stand on the filtration scale with our GFR calculator, but diet decisions should be made with your care team, who can see your full results.
Sodium

The NIDDK says excess sodium can cause fluid retention, swelling, higher blood pressure and strain on the kidneys and heart. Its general recommendation is no more than 2,300 mg of sodium a day, and your own clinician may set a lower figure. For context, sodium is about 39 percent of table salt by weight (22.99 of 58.44 for sodium chloride), so 2,300 mg of sodium corresponds to about 5.8 g of salt. The NKF says your healthcare provider determines the appropriate daily limit for you.

items: Where it hides: the NIDDK lists packaged, prepared and fast foods; processed meats; canned and frozen foods; chips and crackers; and sauces such as ketchup, mustard, soy, teriyaki and barbecue sauce.
Label tip from the NIDDK: a % Daily Value of 20 percent or more per serving means a food is high in sodium, and 5 percent or less means it is low.
NIDDK strategies: choose unprocessed meats, use herbs, spices and sodium-free seasonings instead of salt, drain and rinse canned vegetables and beans, and cook from scratch.

sections.text: Potassium

The NIDDK says having too little or too much potassium in the blood can cause heart and muscle problems. The NKF adds that the right amount depends on how well your kidneys work and which medicines you take, which is why a blood potassium test guides advice rather than a stage-based rule. Only your own results can tell you which applies.

items: Foods the NKF lists as high in potassium: milk, meat, bananas, oranges, orange juice, cantaloupe, dried fruits, winter squash and salt substitutes.
Salt substitutes and any food listing potassium chloride on the label deserve special attention, according to the NIDDK.
The NIDDK notes that canned fruits and vegetables often have potassium in the liquid, that serving size matters, and that boiling and leaching can lower the potassium in vegetables.
The NKF notes that potassium from animal foods is absorbed at a higher rate than potassium from plants.

sections.text: Phosphorus

The NIDDK says too much phosphorus in the blood can harm blood vessels and make bones thin, weak and more likely to break, and can also cause itchy skin and bone and joint pain. Phosphorus occurs naturally in protein-rich foods such as meat, dairy and beans, but the NIDDK states that phosphorus additives are the primary source for many people.

items: Read ingredient lists for words containing PHOS, such as phosphoric acid, disodium phosphate and monosodium phosphate (NIDDK, and the same advice from the NKF).
Foods the NKF lists as high in phosphorus: dairy products, organ meats, colas, deli meats and processed foods with phosphate additives.

The NIDDK says the body absorbs more phosphorus from animal-based foods than from plant-based foods. Some people are prescribed a phosphate binder, which the NIDDK describes as a medicine that soaks up phosphorus in the stomach; that is a medical decision.

sections.text: Protein

Protein breaks down into waste that the kidneys must remove. The NIDDK says some people with CKD may need moderate amounts of protein so that waste does not build up, but warns that too little protein can lead to malnutrition. The NKF says needs vary with weight, age, urine protein levels and the type of kidney disease, and that a dietitian should determine the right amount. People on dialysis may need more protein, because the NIDDK notes dialysis removes protein from the blood.

This is the nutrient where general advice is least useful. The right target for one person can be wrong for another, so we deliberately give no gram figures here. The NKF says plant-based proteins such as beans and nuts are easier on the kidneys than animal proteins, and the NIDDK suggests getting protein from plant-based foods and choosing lean meats that are low in phosphorus, but both frame this as part of a plan made with your dietitian.
Fluids, fats, supplements and calories

items: Fluids: the NKF says early-stage CKD typically requires no fluid restriction and limits depend on urine output and complications. The NIDDK says some people with CKD need to limit liquids because damaged kidneys cannot remove extra fluid, and advises contacting your provider if you notice swelling in the face, arms, legs or abdomen. The NKF counts soups, gelatin, frozen desserts and ice as fluids.
Fats: the NIDDK suggests focusing on unsaturated fats, limiting saturated and trans fats, and grilling, broiling, baking, roasting, air-frying or stir-frying instead of deep-frying.

Supplements: the NKF warns that some vitamin and mineral supplements may be harmful in kidney disease, that over-the-counter products can contain excess phosphorus and potassium, and that herbal supplements should be avoided unless your dietitian or provider prescribes them.
Calories: the NKF emphasises adequate calories to prevent muscle breakdown and keep a healthy weight, avoiding both too little and too much.

sections.text: Common mistakes

items: Copying a diet written for someone else or for another CKD stage. Needs change as kidney function and medicines change.
Switching to a salt substitute. The NIDDK and NKF flag potassium chloride and salt substitutes as a potassium concern.
Cutting protein sharply on your own. The NIDDK warns too little protein can lead to malnutrition.
Starting supplements without checking. The NKF says some can be harmful in kidney disease.
Ignoring labels. Phosphorus additives are easy to miss unless you look for PHOS in the ingredients.

sections.text: The NIDDK also notes that medical nutrition therapy, which is counselling from a registered dietitian, can help delay CKD progression, prevent or treat complications and improve quality of life, and that Medicare covers it for people with CKD who have a physician referral. Coverage rules vary, so check your own plan.
Frequently asked questions
Can a kidney-friendly diet reverse CKD?
The sources we reviewed say diet can help prevent or delay some problems and slow complications, but none promise reversal. Ask your nephrologist what to expect in your case.
Do I need to avoid all high-potassium foods?
Not necessarily. The NKF says the right amount depends on kidney function and medicines. Your blood potassium result and clinician decide whether you need to limit it.
How much water should I drink?
The NKF says early-stage CKD typically needs no fluid restriction, but advanced CKD or low urine output may. Follow your care team's advice rather than a general number.

sections.heading: Know Your Numbers First
sections.body: Check your estimated eGFR with our free calculator, then bring the result to your nephrologist or renal dietitian. Diet advice depends on your stage, labs and medicines.
